content: The calculation of the Universal Coverage Target (UCT) for Gross Domestic Product (GDP) will be conducted centrally, utilizing the most recent data from each country as collected in the Global Health Expenditure Database. Where available, data gathered by the EU Joint Programme on Neurodegenerative Disease Research (JPND) for its mapping exercise on neurodegeneration research will also be included. This is specifically marked as part of the E-tool question Q18x2x1, which asks for the total government expenditure on dementia research, combining both national and subnational government expenditures in the latest available year, expressed in millions of the national currency. The GDO Reference Guide (Page 52 of 74) defines sub-indicators for dementia-specific research investments. These include the year for which data on combined national and subnational dementia-specific research expenditure is available (E-tool question Q18x2x2). The total government expenditure on dementia research is categorized into three main areas: basic research, clinical/translational research, and implementation research. Basic research refers to government spending on discovery research that underpins investigations into the causes, development, detection, and treatment of dementia. Clinical/translational research involves government expenditure on patient-oriented dementia-specific research conducted in living humans. Implementation research focuses on government spending on the provision and delivery of health and social care services to individuals with dementia. The E-tool question Q18x2x3 requests a breakdown of dementia research expenditure into the aforementioned categories (basic, clinical/translational, and implementation), expressed in millions of the national currency. Indicator 19, which pertains to dementia research participation, highlights the importance of involving individuals in research studies. Participation is essential for conducting human studies, monitoring research progress, and contributing to the research process. It has been shown to provide potential benefits, such as improved understanding of dementia, its impact on individuals and caregivers, and more frequent health checks as part of trial protocols. The method of estimation for research participation involves identifying opportunities for individuals to engage in research through longitudinal cohort studies, clinical trials, successful grant applications, or formal contributions to the research process. Data sources include registries, national Alzheimer’s associations, NGOs, national regulatory authorities, and universities. The involvement of people with dementia in the research process is assessed through E-tool question Q19x1, which asks whether individuals with dementia are involved in research development (e.g., setting priorities, grant applications, or research reviews). Responses range from Not at all to Frequently. Indicator 20 measures the annual published dementia research output in peer-reviewed and indexed journals as a proxy for the volume and quality of dementia research conducted in a country. This indirectly reflects a country’s commitment to dementia research, which ultimately impacts individuals with dementia and their caregivers. The estimation method involves centrally conducted literature searches stratified by country of origin every two years. Data is sourced from PubMed and WHO’s Global Index Medicus, capturing research output from high-income and lowto middle-income countries, respectively. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Indicator 21 estimates the population prevalence rate of dementia, defined as the number of existing cases stratified by age and sex. This is determined through systematic reviews of prevalence studies conducted worldwide, coded for study design and quality. Population-based studies of dementia prevalence among individuals aged 60 years and older are included, with data extracted for ageand gender-specific prevalence. Meta-analyses are conducted where sufficient data exists, while Delphi consensus estimates are applied in data-deficient regions. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Indicator 22 estimates the population-based incidence rate of dementia, defined as the number of new cases stratified by age and sex. Systematic reviews of incidence studies are conducted, with data coded for study design and quality. Population-based studies of dementia incidence among individuals aged 60 years and older are included. Meta-analyses are performed where data is sufficient, and Delphi consensus estimates are used in data-deficient regions. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Indicator 23 tracks total deaths due to Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, ranking dementia among other causes of death in adults aged 60 years and older. Indicator 24 calculates Years of Life Lost (YLLs) due to premature mortality from dementia, using the formula YLL = N x L, where N is the number of deaths and L is the standard life expectancy at the age of death. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Indicator 25 measures Years of Life Lived with Disability (YLDs) due to dementia. YLD is calculated as YLD = I x DW x L, where I is the number of incident cases, DW is the disability weight, and L is the average duration of the disease. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Indicator 26 calculates Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) due to dementia, a composite measure of disease burden that combines YLLs and YLDs. This summarizes the effects of dementia on both the quantity (premature mortality) and quality of life (disability). Population surveys are used to assess the disability weights of dementia by severity. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Indicator 27 estimates the total economic costs of dementia, including direct medical costs (within the healthcare sector), direct social costs (paid and professional home care, residential and nursing home care), and informal care costs (unpaid). Costs are estimated at the country level using literature searches for cost-of-illness studies and aggregated to summarize worldwide costs. Per capita costs are calculated and divided into the three subcategories. Informal care costs are valued using an opportunity cost approach, based on the average wage for each country. Extrapolations are made for regions or countries with unavailable data, adjusting for GDP per person. Results are reported by WHO at global, regional, and national levels. Finally, growing evidence suggests that dementia shares several modifiable risk factors with other non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as physical inactivity, obesity, and tobacco use.
